samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Stanley E. Paskan was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Stanley E. Paskan. Mr. Paskan was in the U.S. Army Air Corps 90th Bomb Group, 400th Bomb Squadron; that's the Jolly Roger Squadron. Mr. Paskan was the tail gunner on a B-24. He served in the Southwest Pacific, and his highest rank was staff sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and we recorded this at Mr. Paskan's home in Concord Township, Ohio, on May 14th, 2001. Stan's age at the time was 79.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: I was inducted into the Service. However, when the War occurred, all my buddies in high school, they -- they went off and wanted to get into the Marines. And -- And I -- I tried to get into the Marines. Came to Cleveland. And they said I was rejected because I had a perforated -- perforated eardrum. So there was a reason -- there's a reason for everything. And to make a long story short, when I came back from overseas, the fellows that went into Guadalcanal were in the first wave of Marines, they were one -- about one or two pancakes short of a full deck. And -- And I had all my faculties. And that -- I was really -- I thanked God for that part. So I don't know how you want me to go through this.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I want you to basically -- It's not -- It's not necessarily an interview. But talk about whatever you want to talk about.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'll have questions --

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- along the way ___

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: I -- I was in a -- the surface combustion at the time as a -- a bricklayer's helper. And so they -- they didn't want me to get in the Service. I said, "Well, all right." Because it was a defensive thing where they were making industrial furnaces for heat tempering propeller blades and things like that. And when my draft notice call came, I -- I had went over to the Draft Board. And they -- And the hooker on this one was I was dating the Draft Board Chairman -- Chairman's daughter. And he says, "You know, you're not -- you won't have any partiality. If your number comes up, you're going, man," so... He said, "Yeah, I don't care if you are dating my daughter." And I said, "Well, I -- that wasn't my reason for dating your daughter because," I said, I liked her and she liked me." And -- But when the day came, they called me up in. I had a -- a primary physical. And they gave -- gave us two weeks to get our things together. And then I -- I was brought on active duty in Sep- -- September of '42.

And that was a trip and a half. Young, innocent guy, doesn't know what the outside world was like. And we wound up in Camp Perry, Ohio. And our introduction to the Army food, we -- we were there for about four days, it was hot dogs -- chopped up hog dogs in tomato sauce. And -- And cockroaches are floating around the dishes and things. It was -- It was an appetizing situation. {Laughter.} But then we -- we took a battery of tests. And you either went to the Air Force; at that time, it was the U.S. Army Air Corps. And the Air Force, a separate group, didn't come into being until, I think, 1974 or something like that when it became the U.S. Air Force. So we were still in the Army. And we had issued all our ODs and stuff like that. And they gave us a -- quite a few inoculation shots.

And the next day, our arms -- well, my arms were swelling because of all the things that they shot into us. And we had to pick up two big duffel bags and get on a train. And we wound up in St. Louis, at Jefferson Barricks, which was a -- a training center. And there was a disadvantage of having your -- your last name start with a P. We would always wind up on the garbage details and all the dirty stuff when we were on KP. Guys in As, Bs, Cs, Ds, they worked in the mess hall, under a clean environment; and -- and I'm being made mess hall, working on pots and pans.

And the one day, they came up while we were training. We were training actually with broomsticks. We didn't -- didn't have enough rifles to go around. And I'm getting tired of this. And they came out with an announcement that said they needed aerial gunners for the Air -- Air Force. And said whoever wants to volunteer, stand fast, and the rest of them will take one stepbackwards. And I'm reviewing the options ___. The sales pitch was no KP and all that. And that -- that -- that sealed the deal, so...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Explain how is it that your name affected, guys with the --

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: There were --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- earlier letters got the good

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Well, they were -- they were assigned early; they were -- they were assigned to the various jobs sooner. And they -- they was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Went down the list alphabetically?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Alphabetically. And when you start hitting the Ps, Qs, and the X, Y, Zs, it was grease-pit duty or peeling potatoes or pots and pans. And you didn't have the privilege of being inside and putting the stuff on the trays and things like that, so... I didn't know any better. And then they -- they tried to use scare tactics and said, "Well, you know, you'll -- you'll only live 60 seconds in -- in combat." And -- And all of a sudden, well, maybe, "Hey, we've heard that some of the guys were killed in 30 seconds." And then -- then you start looking at them and say "Did they die before takeoff?" You know, that -- that was the -- the whole crux of it. And they -- they tried to give you other options, like cook and baker's school or machinist, be a machinist. And I didn't relish the idea of being in a mess hall. And -- And there were -- There's some advantages of being on the ground. You -- as in the working in the kitchen; you can eat good and so forth. And -- but -- and a machinist.

But I guess I was a little too adventurous. I wanted to see what it was all about. So I was transferred. And they sent us to -- to Las Vegas. And that's where the gunnery school was. They started us out on a BB machine gun, you know, like at a carnival, these ducks that go by, and they you're trying to get an eye coordination and get some feel for what -- what happened. And then they graduated us to trapshooting. And here's a kid that never shot a gun in his life. And they give me a -- a 20-gauge shotgun. And I don't even know how to hold it, and I'm there, firing away. And I thought I broke my shoulder. And this captain came up to me and he said, "You ever fire a gun before?" I said "No, sir." He said, "Well, let me show you how to do it." And by the time we got back to the barracks, this whole right shoulder was black-and-blue and sore. I -- I couldn't even pick my nose.
{Laughter.}

And we -- we had to do that for a half a day for -- till we got more proficient. And then they -- they put us into skeet. And we started shooting skeet to -- it was to help coordinate and give you an idea how far you have to lead something. And they did it in gradual steps. And then they took us in and showed us -- gave us courses in aircraft identification, what the capabilities of a gun was at 30 caliber, how many rounds they shot a minute, how many rounds a 50 caliber would shoot. And you also (?in that?) got theory of -- of how to judge range because, say, a 50 caliber, they -- they had a thousand yards, 900 -- 900 yards actually, and you -- they had the Norden sight, which was a 50-mile-an-hour bombsight, and you -- you had to mentally figure out as a plane approached you, the bigger and bigger the -- if -- if the wings extended outside of that range, you knew they were pretty close. And -- And you'd have to adjust how to fire; whether you're going to fire high or low.

And -- And one of the things that you learned in gunnery school was the fact that you shot short busts. And in the movies they always showed where you had a straight line. And a machine gun is like a shotgun because you have a -- a 50-yard pattern, it shoots out a pattern out there. And you -- you're hoping that this plane will fly into that pattern to do the damage. So then we -- Well, after we finished trap and we went out to fire live rounds, they started us out in 30 caliber to give us a feel, and then we graduated up to the 50 caliber. And you -- you stood in a turret. It was a Sperry turret that was used in a -- in the B-17s. And then they had the big target on a railroad, now dunking, and it would come around. And each one that fired had a different color on their -- on their bullet so they could tell, "You, Stan, you have the black ones. And we want to see how many black holes you make in the -- in that target."

So after you became fairly proficient -- The thing that you had to remember, everything was compressed. We took -- During peacetime, there was maybe a three-month course. We had to do it in five weeks. So everything was -- Anything that you were involved with, they -- they really cut it down. So after we did that, then we were put on the HE-6s. And we had .30 caliber machine guns. You had -- You had a hundred rounds the first time. And they -- We were flying AT-6s. I never was in a plane before --

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: -- be- -- besides that. This was an op- -- open cockpit. That was something else. And the lieutenant, he said, "Have you ever been up?" And I said, "No, sir." He said, "I'm going to tell you right now, if you get sick," he said, "I'm gonna to wipe your butt out of this Air Force." And the -- you know, you see this strange paraphernalia in the -- in the rear seat there. You recognize the -- the gun. Now, they didn't tell us that it was an open cockpit, we'd have to stand up in the cockpit. And you -- you have a parachute on, a seat parachute, but you also -- only way -- the only way I can describe it was like a garter belt. And it was a five-point hitch, and it was thick. And you put it around it and then you hitch yourself inside so you didn't have the urge to jump out. I'm -- I'm only kidding when I say that.
{Laughter.}

So it would -- This B-17 would come out there with a big sleeve. And the thing that bothered me a little bit was, you know, from the distance we were at, it looked like there was a man in the window and finally said, "He's got a 50 caliber aimed at you. He's -- if he -- And if you shoot -- shoot them, they're going to shoot back, and we're both going to be in trouble." So psychologically, he was kind of playing with my brains, I think. But we -- Well, we fly and then you fly ahead and then you had to shoot. And sometimes he'd bring it in and then -- to give you a better chance offing get- -- getting a good score. So they said, "Okay, when you're done with your" -- And he would critique you. And he said, "That burst was too long. Shorter burst. Shorter burst." And so after we would were -- He said, "When you're empty, you don't have a -- anymore ammunition, and if lift the lid up and you pull back and make sure that the cham- -- there's nothing in the chamber," then he said, "wiggle up and down your gun. That will let me know that I can pull away from the target."

And this guy, he did one of these. So nose up and a sharp bank. And I -- I never knew what centrifugal force was till that day. I was glued to that side of the ship, and I'm clawing, I want to get back in and put my harnesses on so I don't fall out. That was my introduction to -- my first experience with flying. And we had to get, out of a -- a thousand, we had to get a minimum, I think around 30 percent. And the ones that had a higher rate, they -- they became instructors at -- at the -- at the Las Vegas training center. And the -- I always shake my head about the Army.

When you're in this camp, they won't -- they won't give you any liberty. Just before you leave, you're practically broke. I had about a buck-fifty in my pocket. They said, "You can go to" -- They said, "You can go downtown Las Vegas; we'll take you down there." And it was a -- It wasn't much. It looked like a -- some of these cowboy towns where there's a few buildings. And -- And, naturally, there was a -- it hasn't changed; there was a red-light district there. And it was surrounded by the MPs. So if they caught you in there, you were court-martialed. And so you could go in at that time at Las Vegas and play black- -- blackjack for a quarter. And if you got too greedy, the -- the dealer would break you. But -- But with a buck-and-a-half, I -- I'm not -- I wanted a couple of beers; that's what I had.

Then -- Then they sent us -- When we left Las Vegas, they gave us our back pay. And I think we were about ten miles from -- from the base, heading God only knows where we were going; nobody's going to tell you. All the blankets came out and -- and you knew that there were some dishonest dice players and everything else. And some of the guys, before the day was over, they were back to the same -- they were broke because these guys would clean their clock. So we cruised around through Colorado, Sal- -- then Utah, Wyoming, I think we came back through Nevada. We were on the train five days because they wanted us totally confused. So we wound up in Salt Lake City at an armament school. And they ran two shifts. They were -- They were eight-hour shifts. And we were put in the Salt Lake City Fairgrounds. We have 900 troops in there. And we were triple-bunked -- bunked. And so each shift put in their eight hours in school.

And it was -- We had to do that in four weeks to learn all about how to repair the armament, how to check out the bomb bay, the -- the racks and work on the racks and things like that. And we -- The food was so bad that Christmas Day, believe it or not, I went to downtown Salt Lake City, went into Walgreens and had a -- a bacon and lettuce sandwich. But I -- I managed to survive. And then -- then -- Well, then we were transferred down to Tucson, Arizona, where they were forming a cadre of -- and that's where they start putting crews together. We didn't know each other. We was -- Ten men came together. Then you said, "Well, you belong to" -- They named the pilot, and they name you, and you're -- you're in McMullin's group or Joe Smith or so on. I wound up with Lieutenant McMullin. And he was fresh out of B-24s. And -- And the -- the copilot, he was a mustang. Some people don't know what a mustang is.

He was a -- an enlisted man. And he gave up his master sergeant -- He was a first sergeant. He was -- He was a real Army. And he wanted to fly. So he -- he -- he went into the flying end of it. He came out, but it was with the understanding if -- if he flunked out of -- of flying school, he was back to a buck private. So that was a big gamble on his part. And when we were all assembled, you know, you -- you don't know what to do, but you -- you had to be kind of forward and say, "Hey, I'm -- I'm so-and-so. And we got together. And some of us paired off. I -- I paired off with the assistant engineer. For some unknown reason, we had some -- some chemistry going. And the irony of the engineer and the copilot got together and they -- that was a -- that's a story in itself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, let's hear it.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: These guys would -- We were down in -- Well, I'll take you through. We finished our flight training, the shakedown in Tucson, Arizona. And the -- the big test was to go up at night when -- the whole crew had to fly under ___ daylight, early morning or whatever. So we were out on the night flight. The exercise were -- was for the navigator. Okay. The pilot asked, "Harry, where are we?" He said, "Well, let me take my celestial shots," and stuff like that. He said, "Okay." He said, "I want it in -- in about two minutes." And he said, "Well, we're -- we're over Phoenix." "No, Harry. Try again." So he comes back, he says, "Jeez, well, we're over the Gulf of Mexico." He said, "You -- You're full of of baloney." He said, "We're ten miles outside of Tucson, Arizona." So the general -- We're -- We're listening to all of this stuff in -- in our -- on the intercom. And big beads of sweat, "Holy mackerel, what kind of a guy do we have for a navigator?"

So then we found out that the bombardier had his night. And we had 20 800-pound sand bombs. And the -- He was supposed to take a run and drop one bomb at a time. And he makes his run, and he hits the wrong bar. He hits the salvo bar. And all 20 of them drop. And so -- And the irony is the last bomb hit just on the outside -- peripheral -- almost grandma's drawers, he barely hit it with one bomb. The rest of them were scattered all over. That -- That didn't go too well. But then they sent us to Alamogordo, New Mexico, for training, and -- and the white sands. And they offered that base to the English, and they turned it down. It -- It was a replica of the Sahara Desert, but it was white. And -- And Alamogordo, well, that's where eventually they -- in that area, they detonated the atomic bomb. But we had to wear respirators 24 hours a day because the wind would swirl so fast that you -- it was like a whiteout.

And -- And so if you were caught without your respirator around your neck, you'd be -- well, you'd be court-martialed. So that's -- that was very important. And all of a sudden, we -- we had stuff missing. And then all of a sudden, we were introduced to pack rats. And they would come around, they'd pick up -- walk away with an article that you had on your shelf and they'd leave something else in return. And -- And these -- So nobody would take their watch off or anything that was of value; they'd keep it on.

So you'd wake up in the morning and we'd have about this much sand that sifted through on our -- on our blankets. And glass was hard to come by, but they had mesh screen. And what they did, they dipped it into a -- a plastic to sort of keep -- to keep some of the sand out of it. But that -- You'd go in for breakfast, you'd -- you'd be chewing and all you could hear is "crunch", "crunch", "crunch". And the fun part was to have soup, and all of a sudden you get near the bottom and all the guys start -- you could hear all that sand on the bottom.

And you -- How much of this have you ingested? So -- But the pil- -- the copilot and the engineer, their first names were John. And they wanted to go to El Paso real bad. And he had -- The -- The copilot had a Ford. And gasoline was hard to come by. So they figured that if they took some air -- airplane fuel, which was a hundred octane at the time, put it in the tank and mix it with hydraulic oil. And they -- they took off. And they were belching smoke. And about every 50 -- 50 miles, they had to stop and pull the plugs out and kind of clean them out.

They -- They were bound and determined that we would -- they were going to go to El Paso. We -- When we got our passes to go to El Paso, we hitchhiked. And we rode in a flatbed trailer for -- for the distance. And when we got -- got there, you could tell we were out in the sun. We looked like tomatoes. But at least we -- we got three- -- three- or four-day pass. So then they moved us up to El Paso. And the -- the dust was just as bad out at the Air Force Base there. And -- And you tried the soup, you'd get it. And we was -- Then we had -- we could go to Juarez, Mexico. And there -- there was ample refreshments there. {Laughter.} But the -- We had to pay two cents. There's a toll bridge into Mexico.

Then we -- when we came back, we had to pay a penny to get back and forth. And once in a while, we wanted some additional liquid refreshments at the hotel. So there were always stacks of cab drivers that had international plates. And they had a hidden compartment. And they'd put that stuff in the back and drive us over to the hotel. And they made a coup- -- well, three or four bucks extra for bringing it over. So I can go to jail now. {Laughter.}

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. ___

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Smuggling. But then -- then we -- about the time we were going to go back home for 20 or 30 days before we were going to be shipped out, at the last minute -- we had a plane, we -- we had reservation on an aircraft -- they said you had to go up, you -- you didn't complete your target practice. We're -- We're looking at the clock and we're trying to get some kind of ___ he says, "Oh, you got to fly. You got to log it." So we went up. And the pilot got on the intercom. He said, "I'll kill the first guy that fires a gun." He said, "What you do, throw the -- throw the ammunition over the outside, show like we fired something." So in the mountains outside of El Paso, there's got a lot -- there has to be a heck of a lot of ammo, which is very, very dangerous now because -- but that was 50-caliber stuff. But we -- we didn't have -- we didn't have to drop any bombs. But the --

Going back at the time while we were in El Paso, if you recall or read in the papers where there was a Japanese submarine that fired on the oil -- oil field in California, well, we were on our three-day pass and they called us all back. And we had to fly out to California. We landed at Riverside. But the fun part, about the only guy that was sober on the -- on the -- on the plane was the pilot. And the rest of us were sucking oxygen all the way out to California. So it -- the good Lord was watching over us. And even the -- even the radio operator, she wondered, "How in the heck do you work these dials?" But -- And we went out -- we went out of Riverside, we flew ten hours. And we were -- And there were low overcasts.

And we're -- we're hoping that the navigator doesn't get us out in -- halfway to Hawaii and then no fuel. So -- And B-24s aren't very good for ditching in the water because of the low body and the high wing. So you hit the wave wrong, it takes -- you know, it tears out everything. So -- But when we -- when we came back we -- from our leave, with we went to Topeka, Kansas. And you could tell whether you were going to Africa, because they have quite a few B-24s that were painted pink. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why were they painted pink?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Hmm?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why pink?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Because it blended in with the desert sand and stuff like that. So that -- that was the camo -- camouflage that they used for that. They picked that up from the British and so forth. And, well, you know, they had different various tones of pink, and they had sort of a tan for sand and things like that, so... But then we were -- we were assigned a pink B-24, so we didn't know where in the heck we were going to go. And the Army liked to play games. They would -- We had customized parachutes, they -- they fitted our parachutes. And when we -- when we arrived in Topeka, they took our customized parachutes away from us. Then they start -- they had big boxes, crates. They put in winter clothes, summer clothes, and various paraphernalia, so you didn't know where in the heck you would show up. We -- We headed -- We got on board and we started going all over the West Coast again.

And we finally wound up in San Francisco. And then we knew something was -- we're going to go somewhere. But the day for departure, they -- we left about 4:00 o'clock San Francisco time. And it was a converted B-24 that they took all the bomb racks out and they had seats in there. But you were a real prisoner of war. You couldn't get to the flight deck because all of that was metaled off. And you're sitting there, and as we took off, it was starting to get a little dark. And we -- No lights in the plane because they had -- in -- in the bay there. So what do you do? So you start looking for a place to bed down. I went back in the back -- back, in the tail section there. There were a bunch of mailbags there, so I made myself comfortable. And I -- I slept all the way to Hawaii.

We landed at Hawaii. And it took us, you know, at that time, apparently took us six, seven hours to get over there because they were running lean. And when we got in there, it was in the morning. And we -- we had time to take a shower and -- and have some breakfast. And -- And they -- that gave them time to refuel the plane. And then from Hawaii, we went to Canton Island. That was 3,000 miles of water and -- or, yeah ___. We were out there for about 12 hours. And then to look at Canton Island, it looked like a little piece of dog meat. And -- And this ATC where they were -- the Army Transport Corps, quite a few of them were old. They flew the seaplanes, the PBYs and the -- the large passenger planes. And they were -- they were familiar with the route and they knew what -- what to -- how to fly it. And then we went there. And we landed at Canton. And we went into the New Hebrides. And then we -- From the New Hebrides, we -- we flew into Brisbane, Australia. And we -- we didn't have too much time, so they threw us on some trucks and we went up at Ipswitch. And we -- we arrived there in, I think, May --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: the year forty- --

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: And the -- the opposite -- you know, it was winter in May in Australia. And we -- we have our suntans on. And -- And when we wound up at -- at this camp, there was a big tent. And you had cots, naturally. But it got so cold that -- and damp, that I had four blankets under me and five blankets on top of me. And I'd pull the blanket over my head. And I had my oxygen mask with me. And I put my oxygen mask on and stuck it out of the -- of -- of the -- under the blanket. And you didn't -- You didn't even take your shoes off because it was so cold. And you wake up in the morning and, "I thought this was -- was supposed to be a warm..." but it wasn't that. But -- And then we were there for -- You become more or less acclimated.

And -- And they let us into town. (edit with audio) and you're -- you've never been out of the country. You knew what a dollar was, but -- and they paid us in Australian pounds. And like anything else, I would say 99 percent of the Australian people were very, very good to us. There's always that one percent that would try to stiff you. And that happened at a -- at a restaurant. We went to eat.

And this -- this lady knew that we didn't know anything about the money. And we -- we held out the shillings and the half-shillings and the dimes and stuff like that, "Help yourself." And she thought, hey, might as well take advantage of this. And this lady that was standing in back of me, she was Australian, and she raised holy heck with the proprietor. She says, "How dare you?" She said, "You're -- You're a a very dishonest person."

And she -- she said, "How much did she take?" I said, "I don't know, ma'am." She said, "That's too much," she says. Then she took the time to explain the coins. Some of it, you remembered, and the other stuff was going over your head. But after that, they sent us to Charters Towers. That's going up toward New Guinea. And we stayed there for about ten days. And we were -- we were traveling first class. We had sleeper cars. And that's not the type of sleeper cars we had; they had the pulldowns and the big leather things. And most of the time, you just sat on some stiff wood. And the train would stop in the middle of the wilderness, actually, and there's the fireman and the engineer and the conductor, they're chopping would to -- they were running short on fuel. And that's what they used to go -- take us up to Charters Towers. And then from Charters Towers, they took us you you to Tallansville. And that Tallansville was like one of the old cowboy towns.

They had a couple buildings and that's it, pal. And -- And then they flew us over to New Guinea. And we were -- wouldn't even let us fly for ten days because everybody broke out in prickly heat. And we thought we were unique. And they said, "No," they said, "Anybody that comes up in this area" -- well, in the jungle area, it's near the equator -- he said, "we all break out in prickly heat." And he said, "What will happen is when you go on your R&R in Sidney, Australia, you'll go through the same cycle."

So the humidity was great, high. And then -- then you start -- you start the train all over again. And become acclimated with the area, especially the pilots and the -- the navigator and the bombardier. And the enlisted men, we had things to do, too. And -- And we would -- This Colonel Martin, he had a training program for everyone. And we would get into a -- a Martin turret and we'd shoot clay pigeons. And they'd put a -- a shotgun on the right side and then you -- you would holler "pull". And, man, you better make sure that you twist that turret in a big, fat hurry.

And then -- And if you didn't do the -- If you didn't get the minimum, you went back and you -- until your proficiency paid off. And we also had constantly aircraft identification. And if you had had -- pulled the triggers at the wrong time, you just killed one of your buddies. And so you had to be very -- you had to know your aircraft. You're looking at your tape.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't want to ask a question I haven't. Over in a second. I should get your unit.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Information.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Don't want to forget about that.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Okay. I was assigned -- We were assigned to the 9- -- 90th bomb group and we were in the 400th bomb squadron. So that's how -- Each squadron had a different colored patch. And the 400th was the black and red. So that -- From there on in, we did a lot of the things within the squadron because all the squadrons were spread out in -- in various areas because of the hilly terrain that we were in. And we were the last new crew in, so we had to dig our own site. And the only place that was available, it was a -- an old latrine site. {Pause in audio.} Well, graduating from -- from the gunnery school, you know, you -- you would jump from a private to a sergeant. And then completing the armament school, went to a staff sergeant. So all -- all the crew eventually claim -- the enlisted men became either staff sergeants or -- or tech sergeants. Their engineer was a tower operator or a tech sergeant, and the radio operator was a tech sergeant, and the rest of us were staff sergeants. And our copilot originally was a warrant officer. And because he was in -- he was a regular Army man. He didn't go through -- he didn't have a college Education or whatever. But all of the other officers were second lieutenants when we got together. So when the -- when our tour was over, the pilot made captain, and the bombardier and the navigator, they made first lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (unintelligble) (deserved)?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Yeah, okay.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: And -- And the -- And the copilot, he finally got his second lieutenant because he did -- he created a problem when he was -- he was a pilot on -- he was assigned to B-26s, the Martin bomber. And he -- he was a -- He was a wild man. So as he's coming in for a landing after his exercises in Biloxi, Mississippi, or wherever he was, he brought in his plane. And a B-26, you had to land it like a fighter. You had to come in at about 180 miles an hour because it aerodynamically wasn't that great of a plane. And he wiped out 5,000 feet of fresh concrete. That -- That plane, as -- as Johnny would say, "I didn't even come to a standing halt." He said, "They had my bags packed and my orders; I was out of there." And -- And in his records, in all probability, they said he -- that don't give him command of a pilot command. So he wound up on our crew. So...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell us specifically about your job.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: I was a tail gunner. And that was my ba- -- my basic assignment. I did have arment experience just in case. It's a little difficult at 20,000 feet to fix anything, so... And we had two armor gunners. The nose gunner was an armor gunner and then myself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: tell us about that.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: An armor gunner is -- he went to gunnery school and also went to arment school.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: So we'd check out the -- look at the guns and things like that. But we had -- with had excellent support people on the ground that they would -- would take good care of the -- the guns and things like that. And they were proud of their ships. And people don't understand that the South Pacific area, we were there to maintain and contain the Japanese because the -- the big one was over in Europe. And that was the -- that was the prime one. So once that became -- became under stabilized and Germany capitulated, then -- then they start putting resources out in the South Pacific or in the Pacific area.

But we held -- we had very few replaced aircraft. And when we went over, we had some of the B-24Ds that had the plexigas nose and one machine gun, a .50 caliber in front. And that's where the armored gunner was up there with the bombardier. And the the firepower up there wasn't anything to brag about. So in time, they -- they did some modifications of the B-24. They put in the same type of turret that I had, a Martin, a consolidated, hydraulically operated. They stuck it up in the nose because (check) we had -- or, the earlier turrets that they had were electrically operated and they were Bendix and I forget, someone else. I think they were -- they weren't very reliable.

They'd burn out and you'd have a -- a Bendix turret in the middle where the ball turret would be. And all of a sudden, it wouldn't fire. Electronics were -- you know, were probably very fine wires. And so in our group when the new -- they just started to arrive, just -- I was -- The majority of the crew, we had maybe 20 hours to go. They brought in some new ones, new 24s with them, consolidated turret. They also had had a Sperry turret on the bottom. And they took that out because once you drop the turret into the -- the ball turret into the slip string, you would lose about 50 miles an hour. And it was quite a drag. So we -- they dropped that out and put in two 50-calibers on a -- on a ring.

And you could gain -- regain your speed and also better fuel economy. People don't realize that a B-17 -- and this isn't sour grapes; it's a known fact -- they were sturdier and a well-built aircraft. They didn't have the bomb load or the range capacity as the B-24. The 24 was faster, the bigger bomb load. And they couldn't take -- The 24 couldn't take the pounding like in Europe, with all the aircraft. But they -- they selected the B-24 when they went into pole less take because it had the range and cap- -- the bomb capability so -- But in -- in our area, we flew -- our missions were over general, over the ocean, and we needed -- we needed the capabilities of getting to revolve and to (?hall LAN deya and to pinch har Venn and wee back?) and things like that. And so we -- we felt that we were doing our work that was assigned to us. And -- But I had the pleasure of going to the South Euclid Lyndhurst Library where this enlisted man gave his experiences. And maybe what you should do, I have the articles here, but maybe you want to contact them.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Because there's -- in the "News Herald", if you saw the "Spies in the Sky", the three men that were in P-38.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, I haven't seen that.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: I have that. I saw that presentation. So...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And tell us about the tractor, tell us what happened. The latrine in New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Oh, the latrine in New Guinea. We had our -- That was the only area we had. So we had to survive, so we just -- we dug a -- oh, maybe a 12-inch ditch around. And then when the monsoon season came around and it started to rain and we were on sort of a slope, the water just gushed down there. And we were wondering where the cesspool was going to open up and everything else. And our -- our flight bags were starting to float away.

And we're out there in that rain. And we got some shovels and whatever we could. And we're digging and digging and digging. And by the time the rain was over with, we had dug down almost three-and-a-half feet before the water would kind of level off. So we -- we had some ingenuity there. We figured, well, we have to do something. And the officers got some new tongue-and-groove lumber. So we started building this strategy of. And the -- the chief engineer of the crew, he said, "Well, maybe when it starts raining some night, we'll go over there and sort of do a little reconnoitering." And we came back with a whole bunch of tongue-and-groove. And we -- we had the best floor in -- in -- and there -- there was some -- we put it on -- they had some two-by-fours there, so we put -- put the two-by-fours in.

And then in there, before we put that in, we had each individual bunk. You had to tuck yourself in with mosquito netting. So when we had all that stuff built in there, then we put some rise overhead and then we took all the mosquito nettings. And we had some thread and stuff like that, we sewed it all together, and put -- put it over the top. And then down and we built a door and it was -- that was all protected so we could sleep without getting all tied up in the netting. And -- But the latrine didn't give us problems and didn't leak or anything else. But -- But it -- it bothered us, just the idea. We -- We got -- What if this thing starts perking again or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: how long were you in enlisted duty?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: According to my service records, nine months and about 10 or 15 days. So we got over there in '43 and we were back in '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Medals?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell us about your medals.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Well, with the medals, the -- that air medal, we were awarded at -- for initial 100 combat hours. And then when we reached the 300, or the other 200 mission -- 200 hours, they awarded us a distinguished Lion Cross because of the end of the -- whatever happened out there. And the Purple Heart, I was awarded that when we went over to reball. We were pretty well shot up and running low on fuel. And we came in for a landing at this small island. And we didn't know that one of the tires was shot out. And as he came in, the -- the landing gear snapped and we went go -- going -- doing some U- -- Uies on the runway. It was a dirt runway. And I went flying through the air and hit the bulkhead. And I -- I received some injuries, but I didn't lose any limbs or whatever the case may be. So they -- There was several of us that wound up against the bulkhead. And so they awarded us the Purple Heart. And it's -- you know, it's not like some of these individuals that have lost arms and legs and things like that. But they -- the flight surgeon felt that we -- we should be -- since we got injured, that we should be given the Purple Heart. And George kinny (Kenny? ) Who was is the commander of the Eastern Asian, that -- he signed off on it. And when we were about ready to leave, he came over and decorated all of us. And, well, I guess the reason why I got the good conduct medal is I never wound up in the brig.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was good.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Yeah. And then the -- the -- the one medal there, that's the -- for -- at the conclusion of the war. So that -- that's what it is. We were awarded the yellow one is, as I told you, was -- was the two battle stars. That was -- indicated I was in the South Pacific, the Southwest Pacific area. So -- And we had -- when we graduated from gunnery school, they gave us a -- the plane air crew medal. And then we got a little fancier as time went on. We got the -- We -- They released air -- the wings with a bullet in it because the -- the bombardier had a bomb going through him, so... But that's about how the -- those medals came about. At the time, it kind of sorted it out a couple times and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, tell us about that, vivid memories of missions.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Well, two most outstanding ones that I had was we were on patrol. And I'll never forget the day. It was Thanksgiving. And the -- It was our turn to go out. And we -- we were out, oh, about two-and-a-half hours, and my tail turret caught on fire. And that was hydraulic fluid -- fluid that was dripping on -- the pump looked like a -- not a -- going to insult your intelligence -- it actually was like a starting motor. And all they did was take the Bendix off and then they put it so the Vicor pump. And -- And the maintenance on those turrets wasn't that great. And they -- The Army instruction books, they -- you change that hydraulic fluid every 50 hours. In combat, now. So you didn't know whether there was some contamination, probably a lot of contamination in there. And they -- they didn't have the shield over the brushes when it started. And there's always an arc there. So evidently, there was enough contaminant in the fluid that when the pump motor kicked in, there was a big spark and -- and then there was a flame. And I'm in the turret there and all -- all of a sudden, I hear over the intercom, "There's a -- There's a fire in the -- in the back, in the tail turret area that's on fire." The pilot says, "Well, hell, put it out." I'm thinking, do I fall off the earth? You know, is this thing going to -- If it explodes, do -- does it propel me out into space? And I have no parachute and I'm -- and it's -- it was a tight fit anyway. So I would have gone down like a rocket. And I -- I would be down there now. But as I said, the good Lord was watching over all -- all of us at that time. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They put it out?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: They put it out, yeah. I couldn't open the doors or because the flames would get in -- into the turret. So they put it out. And they opened the turret and they said, "Okay, come on out." And I was I -- Was I scared? You bet. And I -- I probably looked to -- whiter than a sheet when I got out of there. And they said, "Well, we have to head back." And we went -- We came back to the base and landed. And we figured, well, that -- our day is done. Then the flight surgeon was there and the pilot kind of cut off his engines. He says, "Get your gear. We got another plane waiting for you." And I'm going, "Oh, jeez."

So -- But that was the best thing that ever happened. That got us back up in the air. And with my own self, I had had about a mental battle for about 35 or 40 minutes, flying. And do I close these doors? What are the options? I could say I don't want to fly anymore. What's the next thing? I said, "Well, they'll ground you and you'll be in New Guinea for another three or four years." And -- And I figured that was no option. And I -- I had said, "Well, I either have to close those doors or what will happen to me when some other emergency happens?" So I finally, after some real deep thoughts, thinking, I said, "Well, here goes."

So I closed the doors. And after that, well, when we came back, the flight surgeon was waiting for us. And we always got a big ounce of booze. So you can just imagine, we hadn't eaten for eight hours, on oxygen -- oxygen for a while, then you throw this big one ounce down. And, man, you could fight a tiger. But he -- The flight surgeon, he -- he kind of kept an eye on me a little bit because the irony was he lived in Delta, Ohio, outside of Toledo. And my brother knew him. So after that, it was -- it was fine and dandy till we crash landed again.

And after the raid on rah balance, it was a big, natural harbor, and the lead bombardier, he couldn't find his target. And the antiaircraft was heavier than heck. And he said, "We're going to have to go around again." And everybody's saying -- you guess what they were thinking. They weren't very nice words. And so we got up there and they were -- they were pulling the wood up there -- the black stuff , the antiaircraft. And I didn't realize it, but on the left side of the plane, about three-quarters of that big star was blown out. And if it would have been a little lower, it would have severed the control cables on the pilot's side and we -- we could have been in deep trouble. I didn't know it and the guys in the back didn't know it, either. And then all of a sudden, we got -- we got jumped by the Japanese fighters. And -- And they were trying to dis- -- disorient you. And they now were dropping phosphorous bombs over us, hoping that we'd fly through it.

And it -- it looked like the Fourth of July streamers as they come down. And in some cases, if you were flying a real loose formation, they would dive right through the formation. And to them, the strategy was, hey, I'm only one man, one plane. If he takes out three ships, that's 30 people. So that was their mentality. And so I thought we were -- we were crazy for flying over that twice. And for having a -- as we were leaving the target, I'm still in -- you know, in the area and I'm looking around. And part of my responsibilities also was to give them an observation, an opinion to the pilot as to, oh, what we hit or what -- you know, if we went on some missions where we hit something, he said, "Well what do you see?" And I tell him, "Well, jeez, there's a lot of black smoke. Looks like we hit a fuel dump and maybe an ammunition dump."

So, you know, that carries over. And I'm looking down there from 20,000 and you could still distinguish a little bit. There's these airplanes down there, about 50 to 75 feet off the water. And there were B-25s skip bombing the -- the ships. And they don't -- they didn't make one pass. If they had 4- or 500 pounders, they made four passes. So they're -- they're crazier people than us. So -- So when we -- we crash-landed and we went doing wheelies, doing circles. And we finally landed. And that's -- And we -- we didn't know whether the engines -- who engines, the right-side engineser were still -- the pilot probably killed them and shoved them down. But I think we all jumped and by ran like crazy. And it's a good thing I didn't know that blew through and hit the ball pit, I didn't injure my legs so that I could run. I would -- I wasn't -- when I was in high school, I couldn't do the hundred-yard dash, but I sure did that. Just call me white lightening.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: After that time?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Yeah, right. So then they put us -- you know, the irony of it is it was a brand-new ship. Just fresh from the United States. We put the first and last mission on it. So we -- we wiped out -- At that time, the B-24 was costing about $225,000 And Henry Ford, they were coming out with a 24 once every 60 minutes. And we were so short on planes that we didn't have a -- a regular plane assigned to us. So we got what -- whatever was, catch as catch can. And I learned the hard way. I looked in one of the oxygen masks, some guy got sick in it and he didn't turn it in. And so I went to the crew chief and I said, "You got an extra one?" He said, "Why?" I said, "Look." He said -- He said a few choice words because he was going to have to clean it out. He -- "I know who it was and who flew that ship yesterday. I'll kill him." So -- But we also didn't have our own parachutes, whatever was in the, had good maintenance on the parachutes, some of them were oil soaked. And they were chest packs. The pilot and the copilot had seat packs. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the seat pack?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: He sat on it. So actually, he -- he was already in his harness. So with us, being in cramped quarters, we had chest packs where you clip them on. And that was what you had. And that's all you had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: about parachuting.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: No. No. Now, the guys in the -- in the back couldn't wear parachutes because the parachute would interfere with the runs and the engineer couldn't walking up on the flight deck, monitoring, and then jump up into the turret. That was part of his responsibility, get up in the Martin turret. So everybody, the -- the only two people that had seat packs were the pilot and copilot. The rest of us were chest packs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Try to keep it nearby?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Yeah. So I would have it close to the turret. And the guys, they'd have it, whether they're right side or left side, so they would be close by. But we had one -- we had to get rid of one gunner, the assistant radio operator, because we were in -- we were in a flying -- a fighting gun battle. And we were at about 20,000 feet. And this young man, he -- we didn't know that when he was under stress, he'd salivate quite a bit. And there were two different types of oxygen masks. We had the demand where as you went up, the -- the valve would compensate for the -- for the altitude. The old style, you had to calibrate. If you went up to 12,000 feet, you had had to dial in the -- and it had this big bulb down here. So Julius, we were in -- in combat there. And all of a sudden, he's got his guns running away. And Scotty turned around and knocked the gun out of his hand because he was blacking out. He could have shot down the wing man. He almost -- He missed our left wing. He could have shot out our two engines. Because there was no restraint; there's no guides to protect. So when he came to, we were out of harm's way, Scotty took his oxygen mask off and squeezed it. And it was all ice coming out of there. Because at -- in about 20,000 feet, you're about 30 below zero. And it's cold enough where the -- the interior of the plane would fill frost on it. So we had to -- we had to get rid of him. There -- It was -- It wasn't that we didn't like him; it was the fact that he -- he jeopardized the mission and he jeopardized the people that were flying, say three -- three planes, a lead and two wing. And once in a while, we'd fly a box where there was one below. So he could have shot us, killed us, or killed the people next to us. So there was -- There was a no-brainer there that the flight surgeon said no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: the oxygen?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: No. Because it isn't the oxygen. The physical salivating.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, the salivatling. Right.

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Because the -- he salivated and -- and it filled up his oxygen mask. So I don't -- he -- They put him into a photography group where he'd go up and all he had to do is -- which was -- wasn't exactly an easy job of lifting a 30- or 40-pound, big camera and sticking it out there and taking pictures.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't fly as high then?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't fly as high then so it wasn't a problem?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: No. Because he -- In some case, he just went on reconnaissance to see what the damage was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of buddies?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: The -- This is something that our crew, we were -- we were there together. We knew we had to work as a team. Nobody was very close to each other because it could be very devastating if you lost a member so -- one of the guys got killed or something like that. And that happens. Our crew was -- Yeah, we were a team. Scotty and I, we would go out and drink and stuff like that and carouse around. And John and -- The two Johns would go out together. And then the pilot, he was -- he would go by himself. And then the navigater and bombardier, they -- And then the radio operator, the nose gunner, they -- they were of a different nature. But when we had to work with a -- as a team, we did. But after -- Once we were discharged, I wrote several letters and then, all of a sudden, it -- and I take that, you know, off -- I don't take umbrage to it, but we were put together for a reason, we accomplished what we did. And we weren't a tight -- as a combat group, we -- we were tight individuals. But from a social standpoint, the pilot, he came from a pretty well -- well-to-do family. His dad had a big contracting business in Nebraska. The navigator, his dad was a -- a scientist at Birds Eye. And he had a college education. And Mack had a college education. And the rest of us, you know, well, we had high school and a smattering of college. And, yeah, honestly, what I can say is the best thing that came out of this whole encounter, the GI Bill came along. I took advantage of it. I -- I graduated from Bowling Green with a business administration degree. And I'm still being haunted by Bowling Green and -- donations. And I thought maybe after I graduated and left the fraternity, you know, I would hear no more. And just -- just enough, how about could you increase -- you know. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting when you came back, adjusting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: Stanley E. Paskan
sp.p: Not -- Not necessarily. But I scared the hell out of my parents because at the time, the Japanese had all the quinine area. So they came up with a -- what they called Atabrine. And it was a yellow pill that was supposed to keep you from malaria and things like that. And now, if you're taking it three times a day, the first sergeants there, he's handing them out. And he said, "Well, I'll take it when I get back." He -- "You got your mess kit here, you've got water in your can. Put it in your mouth. I want to see your old esophagus go up and down."

And so, you know, why fight city hall? Just take it and drink it and keep on going. And when I first came back from overseas, I didn't realize it, nobody did, my whole skin -- my whole body was yellow from taking that pill. My eyes were yellow. And when -- when we reported, we had -- I had to report to Atlantic City, stay at one of the hotels there. And, jeez, the first thing the doctor saw -- saw me, "You're jaundiced. You got liver problems. You got this and that." And I'd say, "Sir, I've been in the Southwest Pacific. We were taking Atabrine." And he said, "Well, let's take a look at your record." He said, "oh, yeah. Okay." He said, "But, boy, you look like hell," he said.

And they did give us specific instructions before we left. The flight surgeon did. He said, "Now, I'm going to give you a whole bunch of these pills. You're going to have to do it religiously. The first -- first week, you take four a day. The second week, you take three a day. Then you" -- You know, like if you were taking some of these medications where you have to taper off. And you -- You're still putting all this stuff into you. And he says, "Eventually, when you're down to none, then you'll be at least 90 percent safe."

So a couple of fellows that left the group before we did, I -- I showed up at Atlantic City, oh, about a month or so later, and this individual came in and he -- he was about 210 when -- when I saw him. He was down to about 160 pounds. And I go, "What the hell happened to you?" He said, "Well, I wound up with malaria of the brain." And that could be very devastating. And then -- And I said, "Gee, I'm sorry to hear that." And he says, "Yeah."

And he was one of the unfortunate ones. He was married. He said, "I came home and I was true to my wife and she wasn't true to me. And I also had gonorrhea from my -- my wife." And I'm saying, "I have no problems whatsoever," you know, I'm thinking to myself.

And I said, "Gee." I did make up my mind for when I was going into the service, I -- I didn't want any attachments. I didn't want somebody waiting for me because I don't know, I didn't know, how -- in what shape I was going to come back. And, you know, times change. Now all of a sudden, this young, innocent guy, all of a sudden he's been in a -- oversees and he's -- and his -- and things change. When we came back, they didn't know what the heck to do with us. So we -- They sent us -- We went to Atlantic City. And the doctor said, "Well, you're awful nervous. You have to go to R&R."

So they sent us to Nashville, Tennessee, to an R&R. The psychiatrists still weren't happy with us. So they sent us to the resort area in South Carolina. And they didn't -- still didn't know what the hell to do with us. So they sent us to -- They were on a recruiting duty. They wanted some guys to go WAC recruiting. So this one fellow and I, we signed up. They sent us to Knoxville, Tennessee. And for 30 days, we had a ball. As I said, they didn't know what to do with us because ample people.

So after going from all of these various places, we wound up at -- or at least I wound up at Lowry Field in Colo- -- in Colorado. And I had to go through armament school again. So they get -- they had to keep us occupied. And so since I trained on B- -- B-24s, they said, "You'll go in the B-17s," and the armament there and the various turrets and things like that. So then we graduated. They still didn't know what to do with us. Then one of the fellows that was in personnel, he said, "I'm sending you to Seattle, Washington." "Do I have any other choices?" He said, "No." I said, "I would have liked to gone to Los Angeles." He said, "It's too late now." He said, "You're going up to Boeing aircraft." So we went up there to Boeing aircraft. And all of a sudden, I'm in shipping and receiving of personnel, not goods. So I got a little travel agency experience with them. And I've done all the new crews that were coming in to train on B-29s, I'd meet them at the -- the station with the adequate trucks and things like that. And when people were shipping out, I'd go and buy -- actually buy the tickets. And all these individuals were supposed to -- They had good treatment. They -- they flew -- they rode in the club car. And they also had -- well, overnight sleeping coaches. So wherever they were going.

But when VJ day came along, they gave -- I didn't get off the base fast enough. I wound up with an MP arm band and a -- and a 45 sidearm. And I'm walking up and down the flight line there. And -- and go up to one of the B-29s, kick the tire, I -- "Man, why am I here?" Missed out on all the goodies. People say, "Well -- Well, what were you doing when VJ came around?" I said, "I was making love to a B-29." But anyway, it -- it was -- it was an interesting experience. Would I want to go through it again? No.
(End of audio)
